level1.text: 1.8 kg of water at a temperature of 12 °C is poured into the tank of a coffee maker. The coffee maker heats the water to 96 °C. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the water? Give the answer in megajoules.

A cast-iron frying pan of mass 2.4 kg is lifted from the stove onto a table in a cabin. The temperature of the pan falls from 220 °C to 25 °C. How large a quantity of heat does the pan give out to the surroundings? Give the answer in kilojoules.
A children's sandpit contains 50 kg of sand. During the morning the Sun heats the sand from 14 °C to 32 °C. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the sand? Give the answer in kilojoules.

A cabin hot tub contains 1200 kg of water. During the night the water cools from 38.0 °C to 31.0 °C. How large is the quantity of heat $Q$ transferred to the water? Give the answer with its sign in megajoules (a negative $Q$ means that the water gives out heat).

A 0.50 kg bag of ice from the freezer is put into a cool bag. The temperature of the ice rises from −22 °C to −4.0 °C, and the ice does not melt yet. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the ice? Give the answer in kilojoules.

level2.text: 160 g of water at a temperature of 95 °C is poured into a large mug. The tea is too hot to drink, so 40 g of cold water at a temperature of 8.0 °C is added. What is the temperature of the water after mixing? Assume that no heat is transferred to the mug or the air.

The power of an electric kettle is 2.4 kW. The kettle contains 1.5 kg of water at a temperature of 15 °C. How long does it take to heat the water to 95 °C? Assume that all the energy of the kettle is transferred to the water. Give the answer in seconds.

A hot-water tank in a cabin contains 80 kg of water at a temperature of 9.0 °C. The electric resistor of the tank gives out a quantity of heat of 15 MJ to the water. What is the final temperature of the water, when heat losses are not taken into account?

An aluminium ladle of mass 0.25 kg and temperature 95 °C has warmed up on the sauna benches. The ladle is dropped into a bucket that contains 0.40 kg of water at a temperature of 18 °C. What is the common final temperature of the water and the ladle? Assume that no heat is transferred to the bucket or the air.

level3.text: In the old days the washing water in a smoke sauna was heated by dropping hot stones from the stove into a wooden bucket. The bucket holds 20 kg of lake water at a temperature of 10 °C, and the stove has heated the stones to 300 °C. How many kilograms of stones must be dropped into the bucket so that the temperature of the water rises to 40 °C? The specific heat capacity of the stones is 800 J/(kg·K). Assume that no heat is transferred to the bucket or the air and that no water vaporises. Justify what the final temperature of the stones is.

At a cabin shore there is a shallow bay with an area of 2000 m² and a mean depth of 1.2 m. On a sunny summer day the water of the bay receives energy of 18 MJ from the Sun for each square metre of the surface. A cubic metre of water has a mass of 1000 kg. Assume that the energy stays in the water and the water mixes evenly. By how many kelvins does the temperature of the water in the bay rise during the day? Also justify why the result does not depend on the area of the bay.

A heat store is being planned for a cabin, in which summer solar heat is stored. The options are 1.0 m³ of water, whose mass is 1000 kg, or dry sand, of which there is 1600 kg in a cubic metre. The temperature of each store varies between 20 °C and 70 °C. How many cubic metres of sand are needed for it to store the same quantity of heat as 1.0 m³ of water? Justify why the ratio of the volumes is smaller than the ratio of the specific heat capacities.
